title: The Weight of Glory and the Two Dwellings
english: It is said: he who seeks his own glory is not true, but he who seeks the glory of the one who sent him, he is true. If we were proclaiming ourselves, it would be suspected that we are deceiving with the word, but if we proclaim Christ and his glory, there is no deception in the preaching.

In the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6), instead of 'through Jesus Christ', through him. Toward the illumination of knowledge, that the knowledge was not found by reasoning, but was revealed through revelation. Instead of 'through Jesus Christ' it shone in our hearts, and the knowledge was not found by reasoning, but was made known through revelation and illumination; for no man could ever reach this, having been clothed in flesh (2 Cor 4:7–9).

Through these and the following, he shows that God does not allow to be tested beyond what we are able. For even if we are being afflicted by those who persecute, yet we are not so distressed as to have no escape or recourse anywhere; for God widens the way for those afflicted through piety, whence also David says: 'In affliction you widened me' (2 Cor 4:10).

We always carry the death, always risking because, being partakers of the sufferings of Christ, we are [at risk] (2 Cor 4:11). The Lord was delivered unto death for us, but we for ourselves through Jesus, so that we might become partakers of his life (2 Cor 4:12).

Because of the preaching the apostles were risking, but they proclaimed so that the believing ones might live, and this is the life in you (2 Cor 4:13). Since, he says, there is a spirit of slavery in the law, but a spirit of adoption in the grace. And he said that we have the same spirit which David also had; the same spirit added the faith, not of the legal slavery. Having, he says, the same spirit as David who spoke according to faith, just as he said: 'I believed, therefore I spoke' (Psalm 116:5). Then, having said 'the spirit added the faith', for this is common to new and old only, since in the law there was a spirit of slavery, but in the grace a spirit of adoption.

If deaths and dangers and temptations follow (2 Cor 4:17–18), how is the affliction lighter? How is it being spent away? For the temptations remained with him and were driving him into old age. How then is the affliction of the saints light? Or is it evident that, being weighed against the glory of the coming age and against the prepared good things for the righteous, even the heaviest temptations appear light to me? And the afflictions are not merely light, but excessive, yet these afflictions fall far short of the greatness of the glory; for the great thing is a body and is heavy. Or he said 'weight' by way of a metaphor of the scales; for the glory, being weighed against the afflictions, is found to be most heavy of all. And he says 'spent away' regarding the temporal; for even if the crushing is long and causes grief, it appears temporal as compared to the infinite glory.

A dwelling, a tent; not the tent but the dwelling (2 Cor 5:1–2); for the dwelling here ceases, but the tent rises up. And he said 'dwelling' for the conduct, both the mortal and the expected. Furthermore, he shows that he calls the corruption and the incorruption 'dwellings'. He says 'dwelling, tent' regarding the body, which, he says, even if it should be corrupted in temptations and dangers through Christ, we shall lay it aside as a corruptible dwelling among the last of things made by hands. But we shall find in the heavens another dwelling, which God provides, incorruptible and not made by hands. Through these things, he shows both the mortal conduct and the immortal. Through the 'putting on', he shows that the corruptible flesh rises up and puts on the immortal; for the 'putting on' is said in reference to another garment. And he says 'two dwellings', the mortal and the expected; and 'two habitations', the corruption and the incorruption, because we are being laid aside from the one and are putting on the other. And he calls the one from heaven 'habitation'—the incorruption from the heavens—since it is not made by hands but is a gift of God. All indeed are righteous and unrighteous (2 Cor 5:3)...
